doc.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01

title: Origin of Eh La Ba and the band becoming the Paul Barnes Band
summary: Paul explains where Eh La Ba came from, D.D. Pierce's version, then the band takes his name and plays New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: D.D. Well, I'll tell you the facts of the thing. There's nobody around New Orleans wrote that. The, the, the, as far as I can, the man who composed it, I don't know his name, but he used to call him the Mayor of Pompon. That's all he said, he was the Mayor of Pompon. Yeah. And he used to sing that A La Ba.
I think it came out in the Creole country, I don't know, that's right. Yeah, that's right.
The Cajun country is what I meant to say, over that way.

D.D. heard him sing that and D.D. picked it up from him. Yeah. But D.D. didn't get the thing right, you see. Now I'm going to give you an idea how he'd go. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. That's where the Mayor of Pompon added. Yeah. But D.D. got it mixed up. D.D. came out. Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba, Eh La Ba. Yeah, he got it wrong and it just spread like that. So, well anyway, we had Nellie Lutcher, that was our piano player, and I can forget her father's name, he was our bass player, and a fellow called Joe, so far back and I can't remember, he was a drum player. And we had a fellow called Al playing saxophone. He left and went to Chicago. And Shelly LaMell, I don't know if you've heard of him.

Well he's a pretty nice trumpet player. He was playing trumpet with us, Shelly LaMell. And we were quite a hit around Lake Charles. So the fellow said, well, Barnes, he said, Paul, he said, let us use your name. He called it the syncopated. He said, let us, you wouldn't mind if we use Paul Barnes? He said, you just come from New York with a big band from King Oliver, and that would be good when people hear it's Paul Barnes Band. I said, well, okay, if you want to use that name, you can go ahead and use it. So they changed the name to Paul Barnes Band. So I said, well, my name is so well known, I said, if we go through New Orleans, we would make quite a hit. So we brought the band to New Orleans and we played up at the Elk's home there, which was the Bull's Club. Yeah. The place was packed. It was a Paul Barnes Band, and that was the first of New Orleans here in El Aba, and the musicians was up there like that. And these New Orleans musicians can really pick up something. And they heard that, and from then on all the bands pick it up. But when they found out that it wasn't a copyright, and there's two of them tried to have it copyright, I don't think they succeeded. It was Burbanks and Ricard. And I think the government found out that they both was fighting over it thinking nobody getting anything of it. It's just traditional. Well, we played around with the band, and I got some things lined up here how the band was made, and that was in 1932. There was Shelley Lamelle, Joseph Pierce, trumpet player, Nellie Lutcher was on the piano, and on bass we had Chester Zardes. Oh yes. Yeah. And Alex Rouchon, that was a cousin of mine, he was on saxophone. Paul Barnes on saxophone, and Alfred Wilson, that's a tenor saxophone player's name. Alan Parade was the director, and Eldris Joe, that was our drum player. Well that band did pretty good. We made a tour all the way out to Mississippi and so forth, and I stayed there for 32 and 33, and we weren't making so much, so I left the band after playing in 32, and to 33 I came and I tuned home of Louisiana.
